title: Getting Dressed
subtext: For when your toddler refuses clothes, runs away, or melts down
script: I can see you don't want to get dressed. It's time to get ready now. Do you want to put on your shirt first or your pants first?
steps: Get down to their level (eye contact)
Say the script calmly, once
Offer a simple choice (shirt or pants first)
Pause and wait — don't repeat
Gently guide if they don't choose
avoid: Arguing or explaining too much
Repeating the request over and over
Giving big open-ended choices ('What do you want to wear?')
Giving in after saying no
resist: I won't let you stay in pyjamas. I'm going to help your body get dressed.
resist_note: Calmly guide them into the first step (e.g. shirt)
tip_instead_of: What do you want to wear?

title: Hitting & Biting
subtext: For when they strike out at you, a sibling, or another child
script: I won’t let you hit. Hitting hurts.
steps: Block or gently hold thier hands
Stay calm and firm
Keep your body between them and others
Reconnect warmly once they're calm
avoid: Yelling or hitting back
Long explanations in the heat of the moment
Ignoring it completely

title: Bedtime Refusal
subtext: For when they won't go to, or stay in, bed
script: It's time for sleep now. Your body needs rest so we can have a great day tomorrow. Do you want one story or two songs tonight?
steps: Give a 5-minute warning before the routine starts
Follow the exact same routine every night
Offer a small choice within the routine
Say goodnight warmly but firmly — then leave
If they come out, silently return them once
avoid: Negotiating past the point of no return
Checking in repeatedly after lights out
Screens in the 30 minutes before bed
Big conversations or discipline at bedtime
resist: I know you want to stay up. It's still time for sleep. I love you. Goodnight.
resist_note: Say it once, calmly, then leave — don't re-enter for requests
tip_instead_of: I've told you a hundred times!
tip_try: Same steps, same order, same time — every single night

title: Full Tantrum
subtext: For when they're completely overwhelmed and past the point of reason
script: You're really upset right now. I'm right here. You're safe.
steps: Stop talking — your words won't land right now
Get physically close without crowding them
Keep your face calm and your body relaxed
Wait for the peak to pass before saying anything
Reconnect with warmth before any discussion
avoid: Trying to reason or explain mid-tantrum
Raising your voice to be heard over theirs
Threatening consequences in the moment
Leaving them completely alone if very young
resist: I'm staying right here. I'm not going anywhere. This will pass.
resist_note: Repeat quietly if needed — you are the anchor, not the audience
tip_headline: Their brain is offline — wait for it to come back
tip_try: (silence + presence) — then 'You okay now? Want a hug?'

title: Won't Leave a Place
subtext: Playground, party, playdate — they refuse to go when it's time
script: We're leaving in two minutes. What's the one last thing you want to do before we go?
steps: Give a 5-minute warning, then a 2-minute warning
Acknowledge how hard leaving feels — genuinely
Name something to look forward to next
Start moving toward the exit yourself
Follow through — don't extend 'two minutes' indefinitely
avoid: Saying 'five more minutes' and then not meaning it
Bribing with screens or treats every time
Making leaving feel like a punishment
Getting into a physical standoff at the gate
resist: I know you're not ready. We're still going. I'll help your body.
resist_note: Announce physical help before you provide it — no surprises
tip_headline: Warnings only work if you follow through
tip_instead_of: Okay, five more minutes... okay, just five more...
tip_try: Two minutes. (set a visible timer on your phone)

title: Food Refusal
subtext: For when they won't eat, only want one thing, or reject everything on the plate
script: You don't have to eat it. It's going to stay on your plate. Let's talk about something fun.
steps: Serve the food without commentary or fanfare
Eat your own meal and keep conversation light
Don't offer an alternative meal
Let them leave the table without drama if they're done
Try the rejected food again in a few days — no comment
avoid: Forcing, bargaining, or bribing with dessert
Making a separate 'safe' meal every time
Commenting on how much or little they've eaten
Showing stress or disappointment at the table
resist: That's what's for dinner tonight. You don't have to eat it. I love you.
resist_note: Then drop it — attention on food refusal makes it worse
tip_headline: It takes 20+ exposures before a child accepts a new food
tip_instead_of: Just try it! One bite! You liked it last week!
tip_try: Serve it alongside something familiar, say nothing, move on

title: Screen Time Ending
subtext: For when turning off the TV or tablet triggers a meltdown
script: The show is going to finish in two minutes. When it's done, screens are done for now. What do you want to do after?
steps: Give a warning before the end — not during a critical moment
Use a timer they can see if possible
Turn it off yourself — don't ask them to do it
Have the next activity ready to move straight into
Stay neutral — no guilt, no lectures about screens
avoid: Saying 'one more episode' repeatedly
Turning it off mid-scene with no warning
Getting into a debate about screen time limits
Using screens as the only wind-down strategy
resist: I know you want to keep watching. Screens are done for now. Let's find something else.
resist_note: Don't re-open the negotiation — the boundary is the boundary
tip_headline: Transition activities beat cold turkey every time
tip_instead_of: Turn it off now! I said NOW!
tip_try: After this episode we're going to do (specific thing) — ready?

title: Constant Whining
subtext: For when everything comes out as a whine and you can't take it anymore
script: I really want to help you. I can't understand you when you talk like that. Can you show me with your normal voice?
steps: Stay calm — frustration on your end fuels the whine
Name that you want to hear them
Ask for their 'regular voice' without mocking
When they switch, respond immediately and warmly
Check if they're hungry, tired, or overstimulated
avoid: Imitating or mocking the whine
Giving in just to make it stop
Ignoring them completely when they're clearly trying to communicate
Making it a big deal or a lecture
resist: I can hear that something's bothering you. I'm going to wait for your calm voice.
resist_note: Then genuinely wait — and respond the moment they shift
tip_headline: Whining is usually a signal, not a strategy
tip_try: Are you hungry? Tired? Can you tell me what you need?
